title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array

theory_refs.at: "because it is sorted, a value is new when it differs from the last kept"
theory_refs.why: Sortedness turns "seen before?" into a neighbour comparison.
The keep-rule table, including this exact rule.
Why `a[write−k]` generalises to "keep at most k copies" (the must-study sibling).

note:
1. Problem
   • Sorted array → keep one copy of each value in front, return k (LC 26)
2. Pattern: read / write pointer + sortedness
   • Sorted ⇒ duplicates are adjacent ⇒ "new?" = differs from last kept
3. Brute → optimal
   • Brute: set of seen values → O(n) space
       ◦ Waste: the set answers a question sortedness already answers
   • Optimal: keep if a[read] ≠ a[write−1] → O(n), O(1)
4. Pseudocode
   • write = 1 · for read = 1..n−1: if a[read] ≠ a[write−1] → a[write++] = a[read] · return write
5. Remember
   • Compare with the **written** array: "at most k copies" → a[write−k]
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(sorted array, in place) → k = number of distinct values; the first k slots must hold them in order.
- n ≤ 3·10⁴, sorted non-decreasing.
- Example: [0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4] → k = 5, front = [0,1,2,3,4].

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: because it is sorted, a value is "new" exactly when it differs from the last value I kept.
✍️ Hard part: deciding what to compare against — the previous element in the input, or the last kept element. (For this problem both work; for the "keep two" version only the kept one does.)
✍️ Edges: one element → k = 1; all equal → k = 1.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** Use a set to collect distinct values, write them back sorted. O(n log n) or O(n) time, O(n) space.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: the set exists only to answer "have I seen this?", but sortedness already answers that in O(1).
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Read/write pointer; keep a[read] if it differs from a[write−1]. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. The first element is always kept: write = 1.
✍️ 2. For each later element, if it differs from the last kept element a[write−1], copy it to a[write] and advance.
✍️ 3. Return write.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   write = 1                         (n ≥ 1 is guaranteed)
LOOP    for read in 1..n-1
CHECK     if a[read] != a[write-1]
UPDATE      a[write] = a[read]; write++
RETURN  write
```

stages.title: Reference Java
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ Return the **count** `write`, not `write − 1`.
- Empty input is excluded by constraints, but the guard costs nothing.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Sorted input + "seen before?" → compare with the neighbour / last kept, no set needed.
✍️ Compare against the **written** prefix (`a[write−k]`) to allow at most k copies.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Allow each value at most twice* (LeetCode 80): keep if `write < 2 || a[read] != a[write−2]`.
- *Unsorted input?* Then you need a hash set (O(n) space) or sorting first.
- *Return the count of duplicates removed.* n − k.

siblings.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
siblings.maps: Same template, but compare with a[write−2] to allow two copies.
siblings.note:
• At most 2 copies: keep if write < 2 || a[read] ≠ a[write−2]
• Compare with the **written** array, not the input

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Sorted; keep each value at most twice, in place; return k.
✍️ Trap: comparing with a[read−1] or a[read−2] (the input) fails once you start overwriting. Compare with the **written** array.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Counting runs works but is fiddly. Cleanest: keep a[read] if fewer than 2 elements are written, or if a[read] differs from the element written two places back.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ write = 0; for each element: if write < 2 or it differs from a[write−2], write it.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
write = 0
for read in 0..n-1:
    if write < 2 or a[read] != a[write-2]: a[write] = a[read]; write++
return write
```

stages.title: Reference Java
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "At most k copies" in a sorted array → keep if `write < k || a[read] != a[write−k]` ([[arr-read-write-pointer#variations]]).

siblings.title: Merge Sorted Array
siblings.maps: Write pointer again — but from the **back**, so nothing unread is overwritten.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ nums1 has m elements plus n empty slots at the end; merge nums2 (n elements) into it, sorted, in place.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Merging from the front overwrites unread elements of nums1. From the back, the free slots are exactly where the largest elements go. Two read pointers (i = m−1, j = n−1), one write pointer (k = m+n−1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ While nums2 has elements left: place the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] at k, move that pointer and k left.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
i = m-1; j = n-1; k = m+n-1
while j >= 0:
    if i >= 0 and a[i] > b[j]: a[k--] = a[i--]
    else: a[k--] = b[j--]
```

stages.title: Reference Java
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Loop until nums2 is used up; leftover nums1 elements are already in place. Merge step itself: [[sort-merge-sort#merge]].

siblings.title: Duplicate Zeros
siblings.maps: Another in-place write from the back: count where each element will land, then write right to left.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Duplicate every zero, shifting the rest right; elements pushed past the end are dropped. In place.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Shifting on each zero → O(n²). Instead: count zeros to know the final length, then walk backwards writing each element (twice for zeros) only if its target index is inside the array.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ zeros = count; walk i from n−1 down, with target j = i + zeros (zeros before i); write a[i] at j if j < n; if a[i] is 0, decrement zeros and write another 0 at j−1 if inside.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
z = count of zeros
for i from n-1 down to 0:
    j = i + z
    if j < n: a[j] = a[i]
    if a[i] == 0:
        z = z - 1; if j-1 < n: a[j-1] = 0
```

stages.title: Reference Java
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ When writes move elements to the **right**, write from the right so you never overwrite something unread.
